blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Interpretability often locates concepts by copying part of a language model's state from one input into another (activation patching). A larger output change counts as stronger evidence that this part carries the concept. Methods that learn which part to copy often change the output more than the whole state does. By that reading, learned parts isolate the concept more cleanly. Yet the whole contains the part. So whose effect is this excess, the network's or the method's? Copying the whole state learns nothing, so it shows what the network produces. We prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to that of the whole. A part therefore exceeds the whole exactly when the rest moves the output back, which does not require isolating the concept more cleanly. Objectives that reward a larger effect select such parts. Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy, for example, exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks, and inside the network at most sites. In both, changing only its objective to target what the network produces removes most of the excess. It therefore comes largely from the objective, so a larger learned effect alone is not stronger evidence.
blocks.zh: 可解释性通常通过将语言模型的部分状态从一个输入复制到另一个输入(激活补丁)来定位概念. 更大的产出变化可以更有力地证明这一部分带有这一概念。 学习哪一部分复制的方法往往比整个状态更能改变输出. 通过这种解读,学习的部分将概念更清晰地隔离. 然而,整个过程包含了这个部分。 那么这个多余的,网络的还是方法的? 复制全州学无所学,故能显示网络的产物. 我们证明,首先,正交部分的作用与整体的作用相加。 因此,当其余部分将输出向后移动时,某一部分就超过了整个部分,这不需要更明确地孤立概念。 奖励更大效果的目标选择这些部分。 例如,分布式对齐搜索与跨内线,在几乎所有任务输出前就超过了全状态副本,在大多数站点的网络内部. 在两者中,只改变其目标,即瞄准网络产生的东西,就可以消除大部分的过剩. 因此,这主要来自目标,因此,仅仅一个更大的知识效应并不是更强有力的证据。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
A standard way to study how a language model computes is to intervene on it. An internal state is changed, and the
resulting change in the output is measured. Much of our current understanding of the internal mechanisms of language models
rests on such evidence. This understanding is considered critical for their safety ( Bereska and Gavves, 2024 ) , and the same
evidence guides how models are edited and steered ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . A common form of such interventions is the interchange intervention, also known as activation patching ( Zhang and Nanda, 2024 ; Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024 ) . The model runs on a base input, part or all of one internal state is replaced by its value
on a source input, and the output is observed ( Geiger et al., 2021 ; Geiger et al., 2025 ) . Distributed alignment search (DAS) learns which
part of the state to replace. It trains a subspace so that the patched output follows a high-level causal model ( Geiger et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . Benchmarks rank such localisation methods by how strongly the intervention produces the
counterfactual output, or by how often it does so, a score called interchange intervention accuracy (IIA) ( Arora et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Mueller et al., 2025 ) .

blocks.en:
Published results contain a puzzle. A learned part of a state often changes the output more than the whole state does ( Figure 1 ). For
example, on the CausalGym benchmark, the score of DAS is a median of two to three times that of patching the whole
state. Arora et al. (2024) report that DAS “consistently finds
the most causally-efficacious features”. In another case, Tigges et al. (2024) train a one-dimensional DAS direction
for sentiment, and their code patches it at every position of a layer. At its best layer, the direction scores 109.8% on their logit-difference metric,
while patching the whole state scores exactly 100%. If these scores are taken to measure what the network
itself computes, they imply that a part of a state contributes more than the whole state. Is this excess an effect of the network, or of the training objective?

Earlier work has reported such excesses and related problems, and has proposed causes for them. Makelov et al. (2024) attribute one case to a pathway
that the network leaves dormant, an interpretation that Wu et al. (2024b) dispute. Sutter et al. (2025, §7) note that a linear alignment map can “sometimes achieve IIA higher than the DNN’s accuracy” and suggest that it “may also ‘learn the
task’ ”. Grant et al. (2026) show that interventions can push internal states off the network’s distribution and activate
hidden pathways. Bao et al. (2026, §1) argue that objectives that maximise probability make steering prone to overfitting, and
they propose CDAS, which trains the interchange of DAS with a distribution-matching objective instead. However, none of these works says in general when a learned
part exceeds the effect of patching the whole state, by how much, or where a given kind of training objective places it.

blocks.en:
Our goal is to separate the part of a learned effect that the network itself produces from any excess beyond it, and to
answer these three questions. Such a separation requires a reference that involves no training. We use
whole-state patching, which copies the entire state of the source run at the site of the learned intervention and learns
nothing. CausalGym,
RAVEL and MIB ( Arora et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Mueller et al., 2025 ) already report it as a baseline; we make it the reference for every
method. At the readout, the last state before the output, whole-state patching has exactly the same effect as replacing the
whole input, that is, the total effect T T of the input.

blocks.en:
Our analysis rests on a decomposition. To first order, when a state is split into orthogonal parts, the effects of
patching the parts add up to the effect of patching the whole state, whichever method chose the parts. A part therefore
exceeds the whole exactly when the other parts move the output back, which does not require that it isolate the high-level
variable more cleanly. The network fixes the range of effects that a part can have, and the upper end of this range can be computed
before any training. The training objective decides where in this range a learned part ends up.

blocks.en:
The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 defines whole-state patching and the other quantities we use, and Section 3 develops the theory. Section 4 describes the experimental setup. We then test the theory in
three settings. At the readout, the effect of whole-state patching is known exactly ( Section 5 ), while inside the
network it has to be measured ( Section 6 ). The third setting is that of published benchmark results
( Section 7 ). Alongside each result, we test the alternative explanations that a reader might raise. Section 8 turns the comparison into a reporting check. Section 9 reviews related work, Section 10 discusses implications and limitations, and Section 11 concludes. The appendices give further details.

(第7节). 除了每项结果之外,我们还测试读者可能提出的其他解释。 第8节将比较改为报告核对。 第9节审查有关工作,第10节讨论影响和限制,第11节结束。 附录提供了进一步的细节。

blocks.en: 2 Preliminaries
blocks.zh: 2 初步情况

blocks.en:
To decide whether a learned effect comes from the network or from the training objective, we need a unit of measurement
and a reference. Our unit is the total effect of the input, and our reference for every learned effect is the effect of
whole-state patching at the same site. Section 7 compares published scores with this reference in their own
units.

还有参考文献 我们的单位是输入的总效果, 我们的参考每一个学到的效果是
同一地点的全状态补丁。 第七节 将公布的分数与本条目的分数进行比较
单位。

mode). A pair consists of a base input x b x_{b} and a source input x s x_{s} . Their expected next tokens are y b y_{b} and y s y_{s} .

( Section 7.2 ).

network itself produces at the site. We call a learned effect inflated when it exceeds G G , the effect of

blocks.en: 2.3 Training Objectives
blocks.zh: 2.3 培训目标

blocks.en:
Every method that CausalGym ranks applies a subspace interchange, and the methods differ only in how they choose P P .
DAS trains P P so that the patched output follows the source label. Its loss is cross-entropy ( Geiger et al., 2022 ; Geiger et al., 2024 ; Arora et al., 2024 ) , a linear logit difference ( Tigges et al., 2024 ) or, in CDAS, a Jensen–Shannon
divergence to the next-token distribution of the source run ( Bao et al., 2026 , §3.3) . Other methods choose P P without running the intervention, from the states alone or together with their class labels, for
example a difference of means between classes, a linear probe, PCA, k k -means or LDA ( Arora et al., 2024 ; Tigges et al., 2024 ) . A class groups the inputs of a task by type, for example sentences with a singular
or with a plural subject.
blocks.zh:
CausalGym排名的每一种方法都应用了子空间交换,而方法只在选择PP的方式上有所不同.
DAS列车P型P,使补丁输出遵循源标签. 其损失是交叉的(Geiger等人,2022年;Geiger等人,2024年;Arora等人,2024年),线性对数差(Tigges等人,2024年),或者在CDAS中,一个Jensen-Shannon
与源流的下位分布存在差异(Bao等人,2026年,§3.3). 其他方法选择PP 不运行干预, 从州单独或与他们的类标签,
例如,不同类别、线性探测器、五氯苯甲醚、k-分子或LDA之间的手段差异(Arora等人,2024年;Tigges等人,2024年)。 按类型对任务输入进行类组合,例如带单数的句子
或带有复数主题。

blocks.en:
The usual distinction between supervised and unsupervised methods ( Geiger et al., 2025 , Section 3.6) places a linear probe
and DAS in the same group. However, the probe is fitted to the states, while DAS is fitted to the effect of the
intervention. Since our results depend on the objective, we group methods by what their objective requires of that
effect. An effect-seeking objective keeps rewarding a larger effect, as DAS does with cross-entropy or a logit difference. A target-aimed objective is minimised at a target effect, for example a squared error to the total effect. A representation-only objective ignores the effect of the intervention altogether. Methods that choose P P without running the intervention have this kind of objective, and so does the readout gradient (the gradient of z z with
respect to the state at the readout), which depends on the output but not on the intervention. Our theory concerns these
kinds of objective rather than one particular method, and the effect-seeking method we measure is DAS.

blocks.en: Whether whole-state patching gives exactly T T depends on the site.

blocks.en:
A cut for a pair is a site C C such that the output is a function of the states at C C and of side inputs (weights,
position indices, attention mask) that are the same in the base and the source run. A cut is complete if it is of
one of the following two kinds. (a) All positions of one layer, in a model whose blocks read only the states of the previous block, for a base and a
source of the same length with aligned positions and the same padding. (b) The readout , the output of the last block at the last position. Only the final normalisation and the
unembedding (and, in Gemma-2, its logit cap) follow it. A partial cut is a proper subset of a kind-(a) cut that is not itself a cut, because the output also reads the other
positions. An example is the single position in one layer that most published maps patch.

blocks.en: 3 Theoretical Analysis
blocks.zh: 3 理论分析

blocks.en:
This section answers the three questions of the introduction with four results, one exact and three to first order. We
first show that whole-state patching gives exactly T T at a complete cut. We then show when a part exceeds whole-state
patching and by how much, where a training objective places it, and how large the excess is when all pairs share one readout
direction. The rest of the paper builds on these results, and every first-order statement is machine-checked in Lean
( Section A.6 ).

(A.6节)

blocks.en:
Cross-entropy of the source label, unlike the objectives of Corollary 7 , is not a function of the mean effect alone.
However, until it saturates, it rewards a larger log probability of the source label, and with it larger log odds. At the readout it therefore behaves almost like an
effect-seeking objective in pure form, and the linear logit difference of Tigges et al. (2024) is exactly such an
objective. The behaviour of cross-entropy differs in one respect. Its
derivative with respect to the logit of the base label equals that label’s probability p b p_{b} . When the base label is improbable, cross-entropy gives
little reward for lowering it, and the learned direction stays below the maximum effect ( Section 5.4 ).

blocks.en: 4 Experimental Setup
blocks.zh: 4 实验设置

blocks.en:
We measure every method at the readout and at every cell of a map inside the network. This section describes the tasks,
models and objectives, the intervention sites, the measured quantities and the evaluation, and Appendix B gives full
details of the data, the models, the training and the compute.
blocks.zh:
我们测量网络内每个地图的读出和每个单元格的每一种方法。 本节介绍各项任务,
模型和目标、干预地点、测量数量和评价以及附录B提供了全部
数据、模型、培训和计算的细节。

blocks.en: 4.1 Tasks, Models and Objectives
blocks.zh: 4.1 任务、模式和目标

blocks.en:
The 90 tasks come from six published sources. They include the 29 tasks of CausalGym ( Arora et al., 2024 ) and re-paired versions of its six number-agreement tasks, in which only the number of the subject changes
( number-only agreement ). The other tasks are the constructions of Kumon and Yanaka (2026) , sentiment
templates ( Tigges et al., 2024 ) , SST sentences ( Socher et al., 2013 ) , RAVEL ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , and indirect object
identification (IOI) ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , both in its original templates and in a sentence frame of our own. The
fourteen models range from 124M to 32B parameters and come from six families ( Radford et al., 2019 ; Biderman et al., 2023 ; Ben Allal et al., 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2025 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Gemma Team et al., 2024 ) . Pythia, Qwen2.5 and Llama are each included at three
or more sizes, so that size can be compared within a family. We call the six smallest models
(124M–1B) the small models and the four models of 7–9B the large models.

blocks.en:
In each model and task, we train rank-one DAS at the readout with four objectives, each from the same three random
initialisations. The objectives are cross-entropy of the source label, a per-pair squared error to each pair’s total effect,
the CDAS divergence ( Bao et al., 2026 ) , and the mean effect itself, which we call the mean-effect objective. Training runs for ten passes over the training pairs,
and we keep each direction after the first and after the tenth pass. Counts refer to the directions after one pass unless stated
otherwise. We score each direction by its exact effect on the test pairs. Inside the network, we add a second per-pair squared error, aimed at the cell’s G G . There, this squared error is trained
from three initialisations, like cross-entropy, and the other objectives from one.

Each task in a model is a case . The maximum effect of a case is the largest mean effect that we find for a
single direction. We search for this direction by gradient ascent on the unit sphere, using the training pairs, and measure
its effect on the test pairs. The maximum effect is thus an out-of-sample estimate, the out-of-sample maximum , because the search does not use the
test pairs. The largest exact (not
first-order) effect that a separate search finds on the test pairs themselves is the in-sample maximum , the
counterpart of λ 1 \lambda_{1} on the same pairs. The predicted maximum is λ 1 \lambda_{1} (the largest eigenvalue of M M ), the largest first-order effect of a single
direction and the upper end of the range. Where all pairs share one readout direction, the angle of Proposition 8 ,
measured on the training pairs, estimates the same quantity. The margin above T T is the maximum effect minus T T , and a case has a margin above T T when the interval of its maximum
effect lies above T T . We keep the 1168 cases that have at least 20 test clusters (a cluster is a pair together with its
mirror) and whose interval for T T lies above zero. We call this the population rule . A case counts as above or below a value only when its
95% interval does, and intervals resample clusters.

blocks.en: 5 Results at the Readout
blocks.zh: 5 阅读结果

blocks.en:
We begin where the reference is known exactly. At the readout, whole-state patching moves the output by exactly T T , so
the position of every method in the range can be read directly against it. This section tests four predictions of the theory
there. Cross-entropy should exceed T T wherever some direction can, the errors of two first-order estimates of T T should
stand in a fixed relation, a single angle should predict the maximum effect before training, and cross-entropy should fall
short of that maximum where the base label is improbable. Appendix C gives the details of the measurement and further tests.

在一个固定的关系中,一个单一角度在训练前应预测最大效果,而交叉纵横应掉落。

blocks.en:

blocks.en: 5.3 Predicting the Maximum Effect Before Training
blocks.zh: 5.3 预测培训前的最大效果

blocks.en:
In a two-label task, every pair contrasts the same two answers. Where the logits are not capped, the readout gradients
then share almost exactly one direction, because only the final normalisation, whose Jacobian depends on the state, makes
them differ. A single angle therefore predicts the maximum effect before training. The angle θ \theta between the readout direction and the mean change of the
state, computed from the training pairs, gives the maximum effect within a median of 2.1–5.6% per model ( Section C.2 ). Since the
median angle is 79.7 ∘ (interquartile range 73.1–83.2 ∘ ), most of the change of the state is orthogonal to the readout direction. An effect-seeking objective chooses a direction
between the change and the readout direction. For the mean change, patching along this direction moves the state further in the
readout direction than the whole change does ( Proposition 8 ). Across
cases, the angle also ranks the effects that cross-entropy DAS reaches (rank correlation 0.71–0.98 per model; Figure 4 b). DAS ends up close to the direction that the theory predicts, the top eigenvector of M M (median | cos | |\cos| of 0.89–0.98 per model). The readout direction itself, in contrast, gives T T , as predicted. The angle tells how far an effect-seeking method exceeds T T at the readout, not where the network computes the variable,
because it is measured at the readout, through which every effect on the output passes.

blocks.en: 6 Results Inside the Network
blocks.zh: 网络内部的成果

blocks.en:
Inside the network, the reference is no longer known in advance. Most sites there are partial cuts, so whole-state patching
at a site moves the output by its own amount G G , which has to be measured. This section compares learned effects with G G at every cell of a map. It shows that DAS exceeds whole-state patching at most cells and also changes the output where
whole-state patching shows no significant effect, that much of this excess runs through attention, and that, as at the readout, the
target of the loss decides where a learned effect ends up.

blocks.en:
For a reference that is harder to exceed, we also measure G ∗ G^{*} , the effect of whole-state patching in the cell’s best
context . This is the effect of patching the cell alone, or the effect that the cell adds when it is patched together with
one other region of its layer (any region but the start-of-text region), whichever is larger on the training pairs. The cells
at which the interval of G ∗ G^{*} lies above zero form the route of the map. Algorithm 1 gives the test of a cell
against G ∗ G^{*} , which we call the route test . Its branches show two ways in which a learned effect e e can exceed what
the network produces at a cell. Where the interval of G ∗ G^{*} lies above zero, e e can lie above G ∗ G^{*} . Where it does not, e e can still change the output. A cell is off-route for a direction when the interval of its effect e e lies above zero,
the interval of G ∗ G^{*} does not, and e e lies significantly above G ∗ G^{*} . At such a cell, whole-state patching in its best context shows no significant positive effect. We call e e at such a cell an off-route effect . In either case, e e is inflated where it lies above G G . Unless stated otherwise, off-route cells are those of
cross-entropy DAS.

blocks.en:
The state at a site also affects how much attention the last position pays to that site. To first order, in the first
block that reads the site, whole-state patching changes this attention only through the part of the change of the state that a
head reads. A learned direction, in contrast, can raise this attention even where the head reads none of the change, and
thus where whole-state patching leaves it as in the base run ( Proposition 9 ; Figure 7 shows such a rise in a
later block). Freezing the attention weights, as in path patching ( Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023 ; Tigges et al., 2024 ) ,
separates every path through the attention weights, including the path through this rise, from the paths through the values
that the site passes on.

blocks.en: 7 Published Benchmark Results
blocks.zh: 7 公布的基准结果

blocks.en:
Because part of a learned effect is chosen by the objective, published scores based on learned effects show something different once they are compared with whole-state patching. We re-examine the two results from the introduction, CausalGym’s
ranking of localisation methods and a sentiment direction reported above 100%, and we ask what RAVEL and MIB, which score
accuracy instead, can show.

因为一部分学习效果是由目标选择的,所以根据学习效果发布的分数显示,一旦与全态补丁进行比较,就会有不同之处. 我们重新审视了引言中的两个结果,
本地化方法的排名和情绪方向报告超过100%,我们询问RAVEL和MIB的得分

blocks.en:
CausalGym ranks seven
localisation methods on 29 tasks by the log odds ratio of their interventions. It takes each method’s best region at each
layer and averages over layers. Its vanilla intervention is whole-state patching scored in the same way, which the benchmark
calls “a significantly more expressive intervention than any methods we tested” ( Arora et al., 2024 , App. E) . Even so, the
score of DAS divided by that of vanilla is a median of 2.1–3.1 at every published size
( Figure 9 a, Table 9 ). The released code passes the base and source token positions to its interventions in swapped
order, which matters on 19 of the 29 tasks ( Section E.2 ). On the other ten, DAS lies above vanilla in all
90 entries (one entry per task and size), and the other methods in 76 of
600. With the call corrected, the difference of means and the probes rise to near vanilla on the 19
tasks, while PCA and k k -means stay low on most of them, and DAS, retrained in the same code, stays above vanilla and above
every other method on all 19 tasks at each of the five sizes that we re-ran. 1 1 1 We have informed the authors. Consistent with Corollary 7 , only the method whose objective rewards a larger effect consistently exceeds vanilla. CausalGym itself
suggests that much of the higher score of DAS comes from its access to the outputs, and it reports selectivity, the score
minus that on a control task with arbitrary labels ( Arora et al., 2024 , §§5.2–5.3) . By its selectivity tables, the median ratio of the selectivity of DAS to that of vanilla
ranges from 0.52 to 1.70 over the nine sizes and lies above 1 only at 14m and 31m, so at every other size DAS
is no more selective than vanilla on the median task. Selectivity, however, controls for a whole task, whereas whole-state
patching gives a control at each cell.

blocks.zh: 7.2 基于准确性的基准

blocks.en:
RAVEL and MIB rank methods by how often the intervened output matches the counterfactual label ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Mueller et al., 2025 ) .
The exception is MIB’s IOI task, which MIB scores by a squared distance between logits. Where the label
is the source input’s own next token, as on our tasks, the count thresholds the log odds of that label over its competitors,
of which z z , the log odds over y b y_{b} , is one. Accuracy can therefore show the excess where whole-state patching still
gets some test pairs wrong, but not once it gets every pair right. Sutter et al. (2025, §7) observed the excess as measured by
accuracy.

of cross-entropy DAS is a median of 0.96–1.00 per model, that of the squared error 0.86–0.94 and that of whole-state
patching 0.93–0.97. There, whole-state patching gives the accuracy of the network itself on the source inputs. In

that of whole-state patching at the same cell (medians 0.33 against 0.16), and at 30 cells it is
significantly lower. Both accuracies are 1, with every test pair right, in 317 of those readout cases and at

context ( G ∗ G^{*} ), whose accuracy is not measured, or the size of the excess where the two accuracies agree.

blocks.en:
Tigges et al. (2024) report that a one-dimensional DAS direction scores 109.8% on their logit-difference metric in
Pythia-1.4b (71.1% for logistic regression) when their code patches it at every position of a layer. This site is a complete

models from three initialisations. At 1.4b, the re-run gives 114.7% [85.0, 137.4], a band that accounts

exception. Its band includes 100% only because of that factor, without which the direction lies above 100% for every trained run. In any case, a score above 100% at a complete cut exceeds the effect of whole-state patching there, which is
exactly 100%.

blocks.en: 8 A Reporting Check for Learned Effects
blocks.zh: 8 总结经验的报告检查

blocks.en:
A learned effect needs a reference at its own site. Control tasks and random-network baselines adjust a comparison for a whole task or a whole network, not for a single site.
A control task asks whether the score of the same network drops when the labels are arbitrary, and a random-network
baseline whether a trained network gives a larger effect than an untrained one. Neither asks whether whole-state patching
in the trained network produces the effect at that cell, or how large this effect is. This question matters because, as
CausalGym notes, “DAS finds causal effect at all timesteps, even when the model has just been initialised” ( Arora et al., 2024 , §6) . The reference therefore has to involve no training, be measured at the same site and transfer
everything that the network computes there, as whole-state patching at that site does, and at a complete cut its effect is
known exactly.
blocks.zh:
所学到的效应需要在自己的站点上作参考. 控制任务和随机网络基线调整一个整个任务或整个网络的比较,而不是一个单一的站点.
控制任务询问同一网络的分数是否在标签任意时下降,以及随机网络
确定训练有素的网络是否产生比未训练有素的网络更大的效果。 也没有询问是否全状态补丁
在训练有素的网络中产生这种效应,或这种效应有多大。 这个问题很重要,因为
CausalGym指出,“DAS在任何阶段都发现因果关系,即使模型刚刚公布”(Arora等人,2024年,第6节)。 因此,在同一个地点进行计量和移交时,不得使用任何培训。

blocks.en: 9 Related Work
blocks.zh: 9 相关工作

blocks.en:
This section relates our reference and our analysis to four bodies of work. Benchmarks report whole-state patching as a
baseline, and our analysis extends critiques of subspace patching. We also discuss studies of training objectives
and of methods that can create the effects that they report. Finally, our work borrows from the practice of activation
patching.
blocks.zh:
本节将我们的参考和分析涉及四个工作机构。 基准报告全状态补丁为
我们的分析扩展了对子空间补丁的批评。 我们还讨论培训目标的研究
以及能够产生报告效果的方法。 最后,我们的工作借用了激活的做法
补丁.

blocks.en: 9.1 Interchange Interventions and Their Benchmarks
blocks.zh: 9.1 交流干预及其基准

blocks.en:
Causal abstraction gives interchange interventions their meaning ( Geiger et al., 2021 ; Geiger et al., 2025 ) . DAS and its scaled variants
learn the intervened subspace ( Geiger et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . CausalGym scores
localisation methods by the log odds ratio of their interventions, while RAVEL and MIB score them by how often the
intervened output matches a counterfactual label ( Arora et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Mueller et al., 2025 ) . RAVEL’s Disentangle score also rewards leaving other attributes unchanged. MIB
scores its IOI task by the squared distance between the logit of the network and that of a causal model. Each benchmark also
reports whole-state patching at the same site as a baseline (CausalGym’s vanilla, RAVEL’s Full Rep., MIB’s Full Vector). On
RAVEL’s pairs, this baseline is expected to fail, because the pairs also require other attributes to stay unchanged. MIB reports
that on these pairs “the full vector baseline entirely fails completely” ( Mueller et al., 2025 ) . In the BlackboxNLP 2025
shared task, which extends MIB, featurizers that exceed DAS are reported as significant gains ( Arad et al., 2025 ) . A
featurizer maps a hidden state to the features on which an intervention acts.

blocks.en:
We use whole-state patching as the reference for the effect of every method, rather than as a baseline in a results
table. Benchmarks
with ground truth use models that are compiled or trained to implement a known algorithm ( Sharkey et al., 2025 ) . In contrast,
whole-state patching gives a reference for the size of an effect in any trained model, and at a complete cut its value is
known exactly. We show that, to first order, the effect of whole-state patching is the trace of the
matrix whose range contains the effect of every rank-one method, and that the objective of a method determines
where in this range its effect ends up.

Sutter et al. (2025) show that causal abstraction becomes vacuous when alignment maps are unconstrained. Our result, in contrast,
needs no non-linearity. A rank-one orthogonal map trained with an effect-seeking objective already reports an effect larger than that
of whole-state patching, and for a linear map their §7 observes the same kind of excess in accuracy. The site where causal tracing localises a fact need not be the site where editing the fact works ( Hase et al., 2023 ) . There too, the success of an intervention at a site
and the effect of patching that site come apart. Grant et al. (2026) separate the divergent representations that causal interventions create into two kinds.
Harmless ones lie in the behavioural null space, and pernicious ones “activate hidden network pathways and cause
dormant behavioral changes”. An off-route effect has the behavioural signature of what they call a pernicious divergence. We find such effects for
learned interchanges in unmodified models on natural tasks, and they run mostly through attention ( Section 6.2 ). A learned interchange can activate
such a pathway without leaving the scale of natural states, because its edit d ​ d ⊤ ​ Δ dd^{\top}\Delta is no longer than Δ \Delta .

blocks.en: 9.3 Training Objectives and Methods That Can Create the Effects They Report
blocks.zh: 9.3 能够产生其报告的效果的培训目标和方法

blocks.en:
DAS trains its rotation with the distributed form of the interchange intervention training objective of Geiger et al. (2022) .
This objective guarantees an abstraction when the loss is zero, though “the reverse does not hold”. With cross-entropy, the
loss is zero only when the patched output gives the source label with certainty. This is more than whole-state patching
gives. Until it saturates, the loss therefore keeps rewarding a larger effect.
CDAS keeps the interchange of DAS. It trains this interchange with a Jensen–Shannon divergence to the next-token
distribution of the source run, “a weaker but more faithful supervision signal” ( Bao et al., 2026 , §1) . The divergence is not
a function of the mean effect alone, because it compares whole next-token distributions. At the readout, it ends up exactly at the effect of whole-state patching where one
direction reproduces the source run, and elsewhere it need not ( Section A.5 ). Inside the network, its target is the
next-token distribution of the source run, not the output of whole-state patching at the site, so it can move the output
where the network itself produces no effect ( Section 6.3 ).

仅当补丁输出给源标签以确定性时,损失为零。 这不仅仅是整个状态的补丁

blocks.en:
An intervention that is trained to produce an output can create that output. ReFT, for example, trains interventions
built on DAS as a fine-tuning method ( Wu et al., 2024a ) . Control tasks show that a probe can learn the task itself ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) . Amnesic probing shows that decodable information need not be used ( Elazar et al., 2021 ) , and randomisation
tests show that a saliency map can ignore the model ( Adebayo et al., 2018 ) . Unlike these tests, our reference is
whole-state patching at the same site in the trained network. Apparent emergent abilities can come
from the metric that scores fixed model outputs, and a
continuous metric removes them ( Schaeffer et al., 2023 ) . The excess that we measure differs in kind. The objective changes the intervention, and the output really
moves further. A change of metric can therefore hide the excess but cannot remove it. Accuracy can show the excess, but
saturated accuracy hides it ( Section 7.2 ).

Logit-difference recovery and its normalisation are standard ( Zhang and Nanda, 2024 ; Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024 ) . Attribution patching estimates the effect of whole-state patching by a first-order value, the trace of M M built with
gradients at the base point ( Remark 11 ). The adequacy of its first-order approximation is listed as an open problem ( Sharkey et al., 2025 ) . Our test of the trace answers this question in part. At the readout, the trace built with midpoint
gradients lies close to T T , and on mirrored sets the error of the base-point trace, which attribution patching uses, is to
leading order − 2 -2 times its error ( Proposition 10 ). Inside the network, the midpoint trace is the
closer of the two at most cells ( Section D.3 ). AtP* notes that attribution patching misses
saturated attention ( Kramár et al., 2024 ) . Proposition 9 concerns the same saturation. To first order in the score, a small attention weight α \alpha becomes large only once the score changes by about L = log ⁡ ( 1 / α ) L=\log(1/\alpha) , a change that a learned direction can reach
where whole-state patching does not.

We borrow attention freezing from path patching ( Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023 ) and from Tigges et al. (2024) . Steering vectors

blocks.en: 10 Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论

blocks.en:
A large learned effect suggests a simple reading, in which the site encodes the variable and the network uses it there.
Our results instead divide a learned effect into two parts. One part is the effect of whole-state patching at the site.
The
other part is the excess, which, to first order, the objective chooses within the range of effects that the network allows. This section
discusses what the excess measures and what it implies for interpretability and for safety and security. It ends with the
limitations of our account.
blocks.zh:

相反,我们的成果将所学到的效果分为两个部分。 一部分是现场整态补丁的效果.
这个
其他部分是多余的,按顺序,目标在网络允许的效果范围内选择. 本节
讨论过度措施及其对可解释性以及安全和安保的意义。 它结束于
限制我们的账户。

blocks.en: 10.1 Interpreting Effects Beyond Whole-State Patching
blocks.zh: 10.1 解释超出全国家补丁的影响

blocks.en:
The excess is not an artefact of a metric, as some apparent effects are. The patched output
does move further than under whole-state patching, because some part of the network’s state can move it further than the
whole state. Whether such a part exists depends on the network and the inputs, not on any method, while how far a learned method moves the output beyond whole-state patching depends on its objective. To first order, the theory says when such a part exists.
Under a
shared readout direction, the upper end of the range and the trace coincide only when the readout direction and the mean change of the
state point the same way ( Corollary 7 ). On the two-label tasks of our models whose logits are not capped, these
directions lie at a median angle of 79.7 ∘ , so the upper end and the trace are far
apart. The excess
of a learned method is the part of this gap that its objective selects.

blocks.en:
Each earlier explanation of such excesses is consistent with this account ( Sections 9.2 and 9.3 ).
Suppose that the readout
direction and the mean change of the state are at a right angle, and that no pair moves the state along the readout
direction. Then the direction that gives the upper end of the range has the form of the illusory direction of Makelov et al. (2024) . However, their illusion is defined by how it arises, not by how large it is. The excess does not need a non-linear alignment map of the kind that Sutter et al. (2025) analyse, because
a single direction reaches it. A learned interchange can also activate a hidden pathway in the sense of Grant et al. (2026) . Bao et al. (2026, §1) argue that the training objective

blocks.en: 10.2 Implications for Interpretability
blocks.zh: 10.2 对可解释性的影响

blocks.en:
For interpretability, this division bears on what a map or a ranking reports. A map of learned effects shows where an
objective can move the output. When the map is compared with the effects of whole-state patching, it also shows where the network
itself produces the effect and where a learned direction changes the output but whole-state patching does not. This comparison mostly separates
what holds in published readings from what does not, rather than overturning the readings. On the rebuilt map of Pythia-1b, the path that CausalGym infers from its negative-polarity map holds. By contrast, our re-run of the published sentiment direction is not reliably above whole-state patching at its site. The comparison does change what the ranking of
methods shows. A ranking by effect size rewards the objective that seeks the largest effect
( Section 7 ). The same comparison is needed wherever a method is credited with a larger effect. For example, a featurizer that scores above
DAS ( Arad et al., 2025 ) may localise better, or it may report a larger excess. Whole-state patching at the same site shows how much of
its higher score lies beyond what the network itself produces. This comparison does not depend on how a featurizer is
built. The decomposition of Theorem 5 , by contrast, covers interventions that patch an orthogonal subspace of a
state, as DAS, probes and the difference of means do. For a sparse dictionary or a non-linear
featurizer, the effects of its parts need not add up to that of the whole, and whole-state patching at the same site
remains the reference.

For the debate about interpretability illusions, the comparison gives a quantity to measure. Consider an effect that

freezing attention then shows how much of the rest of the effect runs through attention.

The comparison also qualifies a common inference. When an intervention along a direction moves the output, this is often taken
as evidence of what the network represents. For instance, the success of activation steering “can be thought of as

from activation steering. For interchanges, success alone does not support that inference, because a learned direction
can move the output at a site where whole-state patching does not. Success shows what a direction can make
the network do, whereas whole-state patching at the same site shows what the network itself does.

blocks.en: 10.3 Implications for Safety and Security
blocks.zh: 10.3 对安全和安保的影响

blocks.en:
Interventions are also used to change models, not only to explain them. They serve to choose where a model’s knowledge
is edited ( Meng et al., 2022 ) , to steer its behaviour ( Panickssery et al., 2024 ) , to find the direction that mediates its refusals ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) and to audit where fine-tuning installs an evaluation-to-deployment mismatch ( Konrad et al., 2026b ) . Some of these applications aim to make a model safer, for example by removing a harmful
behaviour or by auditing what drives it. Doing so requires knowing what the effect of an intervention says about the
model. A learned direction that removes a behaviour shows that the behaviour can be changed. Whole-state patching at the
same site, in contrast,
shows whether the network itself produces the behaviour through that site, or whether only the learned direction changes
it there. The steering, refusal and audit directions above are differences of means, not trained directions. Suppose that the
pairs of a mirrored set change the state along one direction, up to sign, and that each pair’s class fixes its label. Then, to first order, an interchange along a difference of means, such as these directions, has the same effect as
whole-state patching and so shows no excess, while a direction trained toward a larger effect exceeds it
( Propositions 8 and 7 ). Here too, we
test interchanges, not activation steering, editing or ablation. For those uses, the same question
arises, but our numbers do not carry over to them.

Our results are dual-use, like interpretability in general ( Bereska and Gavves, 2024 ) . Consider a learned direction that raises the
attention to a site where whole-state patching leaves it as in the base run. Such a direction shows what a patched state at the site can make the network do, but it is also a means to change the model’s behaviour. Anyone with a model’s weights can already do so more directly. For
instance, editing one direction out of the weights reduces the model’s refusals ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) . We therefore expect our
results to add little to misuse. The larger risk is to read too much into the check. Reporting the check removes one source of overclaiming, but it does not show that a mechanism is complete or that a model is safe.

blocks.en:
Because the account concerns objectives rather than DAS ( Corollary 7 ), it covers any method, including methods
yet to come, that trains an orthogonal subspace toward a larger effect. Four directions follow from our results. • What a localisation should require. Causal abstraction counts a site as realising a variable when
interventions there produce the counterfactual output. Constraining the alignment map, for example to be linear,
does not rule out an excess, because a single orthogonal direction already reaches it ( Section 9.2 ).
Requiring that the effect be one that the network itself produces at the site would rule it out. How such a
condition enters the theory of causal abstraction, and which published localisations meet it, is open. • Where a model can be moved beyond its own effect. At the readout, a single angle measured before training
predicts how far a learned part can move the output beyond whole-state patching ( Section 5.3 ). Inside the
network, where much of the excess runs through attention, a predictor that includes attention would show before
any training where a learned intervention can move a model most, which matters both for steering a model
and for protecting it. • Hidden routes. Off-route effects run largely through attention, at sites through which the network itself
carries no significant effect ( Section 6.2 ). Whether inputs, and not only edits, can open these routes would
tell whether they belong to the intervention or are latent in the network. Part of this question is which property
of a task decides where they arise, since more of the effect runs through attention on negative polarity and
filler–gap than on agreement, and how the share through attention changes with model size. • Edits made for safety. An edit trained to remove a behaviour is trained toward an effect. It may therefore
suppress the behaviour through a route that the network does not use for it, and leave the network’s own route in
place. Testing this needs a reference for edits other than interchanges, such as ablation and steering, and
measurements on the instruction-tuned models on which such edits are made.

blocks.en: 11 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 11 结论

blocks.en:
Patching a learned part of a model’s state can change the model’s output more than patching the whole state does. We asked
whose effect this excess is. To first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to that of the whole, so a part exceeds
the whole exactly when the rest moves the output back, and an objective that rewards a larger effect selects such a part.
The network fixes the range of effects that a part can have, and the objective chooses where in this range a learned
direction ends up. At the readout, where all pairs share one readout direction, a single angle measured before training
predicts the upper end of the range, and cross-entropy DAS goes most of the way to it. Changing only the objective of DAS so
that it aims at what whole-state patching produces removes most of the excess, at the readout and inside the network. Inside
the network, cross-entropy DAS exceeds whole-state patching at most sites, and it also changes the output, mostly by small
amounts and largely through attention weights, at sites where whole-state patching shows no significant positive effect. The
excess is therefore largely the objective’s, not the network’s.

方向结束。 在读出时,所有对子都共享一个读出方向,在训练前测量一个单一角度

blocks.en:
A larger learned effect alone is thus not stronger evidence. The three steps of Section 8 compare it with
whole-state patching wherever it is reported, benchmarks can score methods in the same way, and OwnEffect computes their
quantities with intervals, in a few forward passes per pair, for a direction from any method. Which property of a task decides where
off-route effects arise, and how the share of the effect of DAS that runs through attention changes with model size, remain
open ( Section 10.4 ). Read beside whole-state patching at the same site, a learned effect shows how much of it the

blocks.en: Appendix A Error Terms, Extensions and Counterexamples
blocks.zh: 附录A 错误术语、扩展和对应实例

blocks.en:
This appendix bounds the error of the expansion on which the first-order statements of Section 3 rest. It extends the range to rank k k and to a direction confined to a subspace, and it gives exact counterexamples that mark where the statements stop holding.
Every statement, proof and exact example is machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib ( Section A.6 ), except the expected
share of a random projection in Section A.4 . The measurements on trained models are not.

每一个陈述、证明和确切的例子都用Mathlib(A.6节)在Lean 4中进行机器检查,但预期的情况除外。
A.4节中的随机投影份额。 对训练有素的模型的测量不是。

To bound the measured effect, an objective has to state
its target in the unit of the measurement. The divergence of CDAS ( Bao et al., 2026 ) targets the whole next-token distribution
of the source run, not the mean effect. When all pairs share a single code, the divergence reaches its target exactly,
because the patch along the code reproduces the source run. Variation between pairs that shows in the distribution over the
vocabulary can move its minimiser away from the code, in either direction. A per-pair squared error on z z is not a
target-aimed objective in pure form either, because it depends on more than the mean effect. It reaches T T when one readout
direction lets a single d d reproduce every pair, and every minimiser then has mean effect T T ( Section A.6 ). Otherwise,
it can end up well below T T , as in the example above. At the readout of our models, the divergence ends up at a median of
0.91–1.06 T T per model ( Section 5.1 ), but it ranges from − 0.15 -0.15 to 1.95 T T across cases. The
squared error lies within 7.2% of T T in three quarters of the cases ( Section C.2 ).

blocks.zh: A.6 机器核对的报表

blocks.en:
Every statement of Section 3 except Remark 4 , which is a measurement, is checked in Lean 4 (v4.35.0-rc4)
with Mathlib, and so are Proposition 9 and every statement of this appendix except the expected share of a random
projection in Section A.4 . In full, the checked statements are Proposition 3 , Theorem 5 with its rank- k k form under one shared direction and its sum over any orthonormal basis, and the statement
that a part exceeds the whole only through its component orthogonal to Δ \Delta , with its example. They also include Corollary 7 , the derivative of cross-entropy with respect to the base label’s logit, Propositions 8 and 9 , and
the midpoint expansion of Section A.1 and Proposition 10 with their remainders. Finally, they include Remark 11 , confinement ( Section A.4 ), the exact examples and the minimum of the squared error in Section A.5 , and the bound of Section C.4 . That bound shows that, where its two conditions hold and the two labels’
raw logits move toward the source’s answer, the cap can only raise exact effects relative to first order. A first-order statement is checked as an exact statement about the first-order
effect that it defines. The step from the network to that quantity is the expansion of Section A.1 . This expansion is
checked for whole-state patching and for mirrored pairs. It is also checked for a general patch when F F is differentiable
on the whole space, which holds for the networks we measure. The
Lean sources are at https://github.com/tanyelai/whose-effect . One command builds every theorem, with no unproved step and with only Lean’s standard axioms, and
the notes of the sources map each statement to its theorems and files. The statements about trained models are measurements
and are not formalised. The Lean statement of Proposition 3 takes as its hypothesis that the cuts of Definition 2 factor
through their states. This hypothesis is exactly what that definition states.

blocks.en:
Every source uses CausalGym’s format, in which a base sentence and a source sentence are split into regions, and each
sentence comes with the label that continues it. We build each source as its authors’ code builds it, with the changes that
our method needs and a few stated choices. The changes are one-token labels, minimal pairs where the source has them, and
training and test rows from one task. The data notes of the repository list every change and its reason.

These sources are used in Sections 5 and 6 . Table 4 counts the tasks of each source, and Table 2 shows one test pair from each source. • CausalGym ( Arora et al., 2024 ) (MIT licence). We use the 29 tasks as released, with the authors’ mirrored
splits of 400 training and 100 test pairs. We also re-pair its six number-agreement tasks so that base and source differ
only in the number of the subject. These are the number-only agreement tasks. As a control, a second set of pairs differs
only in the lemma of the subject. Both sets are balanced by class but not mirrored pair by pair. • Kumon & Yanaka ( Kumon and Yanaka, 2026 ) (MIT licence). We use seven filler–gap and eight negative-polarity
constructions as the authors’ loader builds them (the first half of the test rows, mirrored, with each label represented by
its first token). The negative-polarity pairs come in two forms. One is the authors’ one-directional form (every base
label is ever ), and the other is mirrored. The authors’ out-of-distribution test file and a test split without
strings shared with training serve as held-out tests ( Section C.3 ). • Sentiment ( Tigges et al., 2024 ) (MIT licence). We use the English templates of the authors’ code. Some
templates differ only in punctuation, quotes or one word, and we keep one template from each such group. We also leave out
the template whose variable is which review is asked about. We apply the authors’ per-model filter to one-token words,
combine every adjective with every verb, and use the authors’ answer pair for each template ( great / terrible on five templates; happy / sad , good / bad , Positive / Negative or pleased / disappointed on the others). The authors’ transfer setting, in which a direction trained on the movie
template is evaluated on another template, serves as a held-out test ( Section C.3 ). For SST ( Socher et al., 2013 ) , we use sentences with the labels and split of the same repository (MIT licence), in its two prompt
scaffolds. Positive and negative sentences are paired at random, so they are not minimal pairs. There are 200 training and
50 test pairs, each with its mirror (400 and 100 in the task’s files, as Table 2 counts them). • RAVEL ( Huang et al., 2024 ) (MIT licence). We build two-label tasks from two values of an attribute, with base
and source sharing one prompt. An entity is kept for a model when the model’s most likely next token is the label (RAVEL’s
criterion). Each prompt is used both in the form that RAVEL gives it and with a start-of-text token. A version rebuilt with
test rows from RAVEL’s test prompts and training rows from its other prompts serves as a held-out test
( Section C.3 ). Many prompts open with one example, as the prompt of Figure 1 does ( People in Cape
Town speak Afrikaans, English, Xhosa. , which the figure leaves out). • IOI ( Wang et al., 2023 ) (MIT licence). We use the authors’ templates with two or twenty one-token names, with
and without a start-of-text token. We also use our own sentence frame with our own names, which carries a start-of-text token.
Training on ten of the authors’ fifteen templates and testing on the other five serves as a held-out test
( Section C.3 ).

blocks.en:
Effects are evaluated in batches of 25 with right padding on the maps, and in batches of equal length on the readout runs.
At the readout and on the maps, intervals use 2000 resamples of test clusters (percentile intervals, and basic intervals for
ratios involving λ 1 \lambda_{1} ). RAVEL’s pairs share entities across clusters. At the readout we therefore use an analytic
two-way cluster interval by the entity of each value ( Cameron et al., 2011 ) for four RAVEL quantities, namely T T in the
population rule, the margin above T T , the excess and the comparison with the squared error ( Section C.1 ). For the
sentiment direction, intervals use 10,000 circular-block resamples of neighbouring prompts (blocks of two), and a band that
is simultaneous over the layers accounts for the choice of layer ( Section 7.3 ). Because there are few blocks, the
band includes a small-sample factor , which widens it ( Section E.3 ).

0.6). CausalGym’s own code also ran on the GPU, in its own environment (PyTorch 2.7.0, Transformers 4.46.2, pyvene
0.1.6) and with the models at their current address. The checks of its token positions ( Section E.2 ) ran on the same
machine. The code, the scripts that build every data source and the Lean proofs are at https://github.com/tanyelai/whose-effect . They come with OwnEffect, a small library that measures a learned effect beside whole-state patching at the same site, with
intervals, for a direction from any method ( Appendix F ). Its name refers to the effect that the network itself
produces at a site. One script per
experiment re-runs that experiment, and one script rebuilds each table and figure from
the outputs of the scoring scripts.

blocks.en: C.1 Details of the Readout Measurement
blocks.zh: C.1 读出计量的细节

blocks.en:
Every number in Section 5 comes from one measurement. For each model and task, it
uses the training and test pairs whose labels are single tokens. At the readout cell, it measures the effect of whole-state
patching, T T , and the exact effect of every direction on every test pair. It builds M M from midpoint gradients
( Theorem 5 ) and computes its top eigenvalue exactly in the span of the pairs. Each initialisation has its own batch
order, and the four objectives (cross-entropy, the squared error, the divergence of CDAS and the mean-effect objective)
train together on this order. The effect of an objective is the mean of the per-pair effects of its three initialisations.
The maximum effect of Section 4.1 , the out-of-sample maximum, is found on the training pairs and measured on the
test pairs. The search uses Adam on an unnormalised vector v v with d = v / ‖ v ‖ d=v/\|v\| . It takes 100
full-batch steps on the training pairs, with a step size of 10 − 3 10^{-3} that decays on a cosine schedule to 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and it
keeps the best iterate. It starts from two directions. The first is the direction that the mean-effect objective reaches
after ten passes, from whichever of its three initialisations ends with the largest effect on the training pairs. The second
is the top eigenvector of M M built from midpoint gradients on the training pairs. The in-sample maximum ( Section 4.1 ) comes from a separate search on the test pairs and is measured on the same pairs. It is the exact counterpart of λ 1 \lambda_{1} , which is also
computed on the test pairs, and it is never below the out-of-sample maximum. The margin
above T T , the intervals (for RAVEL, two-way by entity) and the counting rule are those of Section 4 . After
false-discovery control over the tasks of a model (Benjamini–Hochberg, q = 0.025 q=0.025 ), cross-entropy DAS lies above T T in
1093 rather than 1096 of the tasks with a margin above T T . The mean-effect objective does so in
1121 rather than 1124 of them. In Gemma-2, at least one trained run of cross-entropy DAS lies above λ 1 \lambda_{1} in 25 rather than 34 tasks. Table 4 gives the results for every
source. RAVEL’s plain and JSON prompts of one attribute (121 model–task cases) and SST’s two prompt scaffolds
(14) count as separate tasks. With each construction counted once, cross-entropy DAS lies above T T in
966 of the 994 cases with a margin above T T , with the same 28 misses.

The main population consists of 1168 cases in the fourteen models, selected by the
population rule of Section 4.1 . The rule asks for at least 20 test clusters, which the bootstrap needs, and for an
interval for T T above zero, which is needed because effects are expressed in units of T T . Both
conditions are fixed before any training and do not depend on any trained direction. Of the tasks with data, the
two conditions leave out 19 model–task cases. Of these, 14 have 10–18 test clusters. Some of
them are sentiment templates, where the one-token word filter leaves fewer sentences. These are one template in each of Pythia-160m, 410m, 1b and 6.9b, four templates in SmolLM2-360M and the book-review template in GPT-2 and Gemma-2. The others are four
RAVEL attributes, in Pythia-1b, Pythia-6.9b and Llama-3.2-1B (two). In these cases, cross-entropy DAS lies at
1.2–3.4 T T , as it does elsewhere. In the remaining 5 cases, the input does not change the output in the
way that the labels assume. Two of them are the filler_gap_embed_4 tasks of Qwen2.5-0.5B and Pythia-160m, and one
is Llama-3.2-3B’s JSON prompt of a city’s latitude. The intervals for T T of these three include zero (for RAVEL, by the
two-way interval). The other two are Gemma-2’s two IOI tasks on the templates of Wang et al. (2023) , with T T at − 15.2 -15.2 and − 14.6 -14.6 .
Gemma-2 expects a start-of-text token, which the prompts of RAVEL and IOI lack in the form that their sources use. Without
this token, Gemma-2 names the wrong person on those templates, and too few RAVEL prompts give both answers, so only
8 of the population’s 24 RAVEL tasks are built. With the token, its IOI T T is 10.7–12.9, and
23 RAVEL tasks are built. Cross-entropy DAS then lies above T T in 22 of the 23
RAVEL tasks, and the remaining one has no margin above T T . It also lies above T T in the two-name IOI task
(1.53 T T ), and the twenty-name task has no margin above T T . In Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B, RAVEL’s

value. Including the left-out tasks would add only tasks in which cross-entropy DAS lies above T T , or ratios whose
denominator T T is near or below zero.

Every identity that the measurement relies on is checked by comparing two float32 computations
of the same quantity. The first two comparisons are between the logits computed from the readout and the model’s logits, and
between T T from the readout and T T from the forward pass. The other two are between the effect of whole-state patching at
the readout cell and T T , and between an unpatched run with attention frozen and the base run. In each comparison, the two
values must agree within the rounding error of a float32 dot product as long as the model’s width, for results as large as
the model’s logits. This tolerance is 2 ​ γ D ​ o max 2\gamma_{D}\,o_{\max} for a logit and 8 ​ γ D ​ o max 8\gamma_{D}\,o_{\max} for an effect, with γ D = D ​ u / ( 1 − D ​ u ) \gamma_{D}=Du/(1-Du) , u = 2 − 24 u=2^{-24} and D D the hidden size. Here o max o_{\max} is the largest | | label logit | | over a sample
of test inputs (up to ten rows per task in the six small models and three in the others; for Qwen2.5-32B, the saved logits of

blocks.en: C.2 Training Losses and the First-Order Approximation
blocks.zh: C.2 培训损失和第一订单

blocks.en:
After ten passes, cross-entropy DAS lies above T T in 1102
of the 1124 cases with a margin above T T , at 0.81–0.98 of the maximum effect (0.76–0.97 after one pass). Its
runs from the three initialisations reach the same direction (median | cos | |\cos| 0.995 at ten passes and
0.979 at one). We also optimised its objective exactly from the top eigenvector of M M ( Theorem 5 ), a
starting point unrelated to its training. In each of the fourteen models, the median | cos | |\cos| between this optimum and
DAS is 0.986–0.998, and the optimum has a median of 0.3–2.2% more effect than DAS. In the 7–32B models, a tenth of the
tasks gain more than 3–13% per model, and none gains more than 24%. Most of the distance
between DAS and the maximum effect is due to the objective, not to unfinished training. We also applied the first-order
approximation before training to the measure of cross-entropy itself, log ⁡ p ⁡ ( y s ) \log p(y_{s}) . Outside the negative-polarity tasks, it
does not predict the size of this distance. Whether it predicts the direction of this distance cannot be tested. In every
task, at least one of the two directions that such a test would compare, the first-order optimum and the mean-effect direction,
deviates from the top eigenvector of M M by an angle whose sine is below 0.05. A deviation this small does not define a
direction. On mirrored test sets, the first-order optimum coincides with this eigenvector. There, a pair and
its mirror cancel the softmax terms, so the first-order value of log ⁡ p ⁡ ( y s ) \log p(y_{s}) is half that of the log odds, and the same
direction maximises both. The first-order approximation thus predicts no deviation from the top eigenvector, while
cross-entropy DAS deviates from it by a median sine of 0.15–0.44 per model.

With the squared error, three quarters of the 1168 cases lie within
7.2% of T T . Cross-entropy DAS lies above the squared error in 1102 of the 1124 cases with a
margin above T T . All the other cases are one-directional negative-polarity tasks, and in all but one of them (Llama-3.2-1B’s NPIOnly ), cross-entropy DAS does not lie above T T . The squared error lies farther from T T on the sentiment
templates ( Table 4 ) and on IOI with twenty names, where the maximum effect itself lies below T T . In all
27 cases whose maximum effect lies below T T , cross-entropy DAS stays below T T , as the second counterexample of Section A.5 , in which the maximum lies below T T , predicts. The data do not show that the squared error reaches the
first-order optimum of its loss instead of T T .
Where the two differ, T T is significantly closer in 4–43 tasks per model, although the optimum is closer in more
tasks, 5–30 per model (236 against 170 of the 839 tasks, and
43 of the tasks where T T is closer are Gemma-2’s). The trained direction is far from that optimum (median | cos | |\cos| 0.50), and the two predicted values are a few percent apart. One pass leaves the squared error short of
convergence. After ten passes, it ends up a median of 2.4% from T T (three quarters within
5.0%). On the sentiment templates, which train for a median of 25 steps per pass against
100 elsewhere, it ends up 4.4% from T T after ten passes, against 8.4% after one. The divergence
of CDAS ends up at 0.95–1.08 T T per model after ten passes.

DAS is evaluated on held-out pairs. This tests whether a direction generalises across inputs, not which path its effect
takes. Write the effect of a direction d d on the pairs of entity ϵ \epsilon as e ϵ ​ ( d ) = s ⁡ ( d ) + r ϵ ​ ( d ) e_{\epsilon}(d)=s(d)+r_{\epsilon}(d) , where s ⁡ ( d ) = 𝔼 ϵ ​ [ e ϵ ​ ( d ) ] s(d)=\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}[e_{\epsilon}(d)] is the part shared across entities. Held-out evaluation thus removes the entity-specific part r ϵ r_{\epsilon} , but not the shared part s s , which
includes any change of the output that is common to all entities. If a direction raises the attention to the site on every
entity alike, the effect of this rise is part of s s , and so is a shift toward the upper end of the range that every entity
shares. Both survive held-out evaluation as fully as the part of the effect that whole-state patching also produces. We test
held-out templates at the readout only. There, neither they nor held-out prompts remove this shift. On IOI’s held-out
templates, cross-entropy DAS lies above T T in all 13 cases of the task with two names. On RAVEL’s test prompts, it
lies above T T in 223 of the 224 cases with a margin above T T , and on the split of Kumon and Yanaka
without shared strings in 172 of 196 such cases. When the test pairs differ from the training
pairs in construction or template, the margin above T T itself often disappears. It remains in 97 of
210 cases on the out-of-distribution test set of Kumon and Yanaka, and in 60 of 121 cases on the
sentiment transfer test, which evaluates a direction trained on the movie template on another template. Cross-entropy DAS
ends up at a median of 0.45 T T and 0.83 T T on these two tests. Where the margin remains, cross-entropy DAS
lies above T T in 90 of these cases on the first test and in 54 on the second. Out-of-distribution
tests thus remove the excess mainly where they remove the margin above T T itself.

difference follows from a theorem. Suppose that a label’s raw logit

change is at least as large in size as the raw change times the cap’s slope at the bent midpoint (by Hermite–Hadamard for ψ ′ \psi^{\prime} , then by the bend). Where the source label’s raw logit rises and the base label’s falls, the cap can therefore only

blocks.en:
Comparing small and large models across families mixes size with training data, tokeniser and architecture. Our
statements about size therefore rest on a test within families. The test of Section 5.4 compares three sizes within each family, whose models share one tokeniser. These are Pythia 410m,
1b and 6.9b; Qwen2.5 0.5B, 1.5B and 7B; and Llama 3.2-1B, 3.2-3B and 3.1-8B. In Qwen2.5, the test takes one further step,
from 7B to 32B. Pythia-160m, which is smaller than the three sizes, is drawn on its family’s line in Figure 4 c. On
each task of the common set of a family, we take the maximum effect (the out-of-sample maximum over T T ), cross-entropy DAS
(its effect over T T ) and the share of the maximum that cross-entropy reaches (the ratio of the two). We compare sizes by the
median per-task log ratio, with a task bootstrap. The test asks that a larger model have a larger margin above T T and
that cross-entropy DAS report a larger excess in it. For each of these two quantities, the interval of the median log ratio
must lie above zero at both steps up from the smallest size, to the middle size and to the largest. The test also asks that
cross-entropy take a smaller share of the maximum from the smallest to the largest of the three sizes. The step from
Qwen2.5-7B to 32B is held to the same three conditions.

blocks.en:
The test has three limits. First, the step between the two smaller sizes of Qwen2.5 and Llama, whose
embeddings are tied, is small and rests on CausalGym’s tasks; without these tasks, the growth at that step does not hold.
Second, most of the growth comes with the largest of the three sizes, where the embeddings are untied and, in Llama, the
model is the one from which the two smaller models were pruned and distilled. These steps do not separate size from those
changes. However, Pythia, which never ties its embeddings, grows at about the same rate per doubling at both steps, and
Qwen2.5 still grows from 7B to 32B, with untied embeddings at both sizes. Third, the growth is uneven across sources

This appendix describes the maps behind Section 6 , with their cells, counts and controls. It also reports every
further test of the findings of that section.

blocks.en:
The full grid holds 78 tasks in the six small models. These are CausalGym’s 29
tasks and 49 tasks from the other sources (Kumon and Yanaka’s constructions, number-only agreement, RAVEL, IOI, SST and the
sentiment templates). The population rule of Section 4.1 leaves out eight maps, and 460 remain. The maps left out are
those of sentiment templates with fewer than 20 test clusters and those of filler_gap_embed_4 in Qwen2.5-0.5B and
Pythia-160m, whose interval for T T does not lie above zero. Every
count excludes the 2065 cells whose region is empty in some row, where the patch would take the token of another region. A cell is live when, in some
pair, base and source differ in at least one token up to that cell. At each live cell, we measure on test pairs the effect of
whole-state patching, G G , and its value in the best context, G ∗ G^{*} , with the context chosen on the training pairs. A cell is
off-route ( Algorithm 1 ) when the interval of DAS lies above zero, the interval of G ∗ G^{*} does not, and DAS lies significantly above G ∗ G^{*} .
There are 4300 such cells. At 152 more cells, the interval of DAS lies above zero and that of G ∗ G^{*} does not, but the difference between DAS and G ∗ G^{*} is not significant. We also measure cross-entropy DAS and the squared error aimed at G G from three initialisations, the mean-effect
objective, the squared error aimed at T T and the CDAS divergence from one initialisation, and the untrained directions. Each is
measured twice, once with attention free to change and once with every downstream attention pattern frozen to that of the
base run. The first-order range comes from the midpoint gradients of the test pairs, computed before any training. Intervals
resample mirrored pairs together. Correlations are averaged across maps, which serve as the units. Cell counts use per-cell
intervals after false-discovery control over the cells of each model (Benjamini–Hochberg, q = 0.025 q=0.025 , with p p -values from
the standard error of the resampling). The exception is the off-route cells, which are counted on raw intervals (4300,
and 4270 after the control). On raw intervals, the counts are 16,560 cells above G G ,
16,099 above G ∗ G^{*} and 5872 above the predicted maximum, against 16,489, 15,998 and
4894 after the control.

blocks.en: D.2 The Large Models

blocks.en:
The four large models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen2.5-7B and Pythia-6.9b) were mapped on three of CausalGym’s tasks,
negative polarity, filler–gap and subject–verb agreement, at every second layer and at the readout. Their results are
close to those in the small models. Three maps per model are too few for a test, because a bootstrap’s 2.5% quantile over
three maps would be the smallest map itself. We therefore describe these maps without a test across maps, and we compare
them with the small models on the same tasks. DAS lies significantly above G G at 1322 of the 1352 live
cells (with false-discovery control per model), against 1190 of 1218 in the small models. Per model,
Gemma-2 included, 0.58–0.71 of the effect of DAS summed over live cells lies beyond G ∗ G^{*} , the effect of
whole-state patching in its best context, and 0.65–0.71 in the three models whose logits are not capped. The
share in the small models is 0.56–0.65 per model. Of the part beyond G ∗ G^{*} , 0.61–0.71 runs through attention in
the uncapped models (0.57–0.72 in the small models). Gemma-2, whose logits are capped, gives 0.58 and
0.61. It is left out of the shares of the uncapped models, but the count of cells above G G includes it.

blocks.en:
This appendix gives the details behind Section 7 . It covers the rebuilt CausalGym maps, the re-run of CausalGym’s
corrected code and the re-run of the sentiment direction.

blocks.en: E.1 Rebuilding CausalGym’s Maps
blocks.zh: E.1 重建因果基因图

blocks.en:
We rebuilt CausalGym’s maps for its 29 tasks in the six small models, at every layer
(174 maps, Section 4.2 ). We follow the benchmark’s protocol, that is, the rows as published, the first token of
each label, one epoch, batch size 4, Adam at 5 ⋅ 10 − 3 5\cdot 10^{-3} and cross-entropy of the source label. We use three
initialisations, a constant learning rate, float32 and a renormalised direction. CausalGym’s paper instead uses one
initialisation, a linear schedule with warmup, bfloat16 at 1b (float32 up to 410m) and pyvene’s orthogonally parametrised
rotation. In the three models with published values, we compare with these values on the ten tasks that the released code reads
correctly ( Section E.2 ). Our vanilla score equals the published one to its two decimals in 25 of 30 cases and differs
by 0.01 in the rest. In 28 cases, the published DAS value lies within the 95% resampling range of our aggregate
for a single initialisation, with the resamples of the three initialisations pooled.
Pythia-1b’s negative-polarity DAS map matches Figure 5(b) of CausalGym’s paper layer by layer (Spearman 0.99, against
0.95 with the layers offset by one).

blocks.en:
In the published scores, the difference of means lies at the level of vanilla on the ten tasks whose positions coincide
(median 0.96–1.00 per size) and at 0.54–0.71 on the other 19 ( Figure 9 a). Since the
ten are exactly the negative-polarity and filler–gap tasks, this difference could also come from the kind of task. We
therefore re-ran the authors’ code on the five Pythia sizes up to 410m, once as released and once with the two positions in
order, on the 19 tasks and on two of the ten as controls. As released, the code reproduces the published scores at 70m, 160m
and 410m to the second decimal on all 19 tasks (LDA on 11–18); at 14m and 31m, the weights at the published address
were replaced in February 2026, so the published values cannot serve as a reference there. On the controls, the
deterministic methods give identical rows in both conditions. With the positions in order, the difference of means rises
from a median of 0.58–0.78 of vanilla to 0.96–0.98 and the probes reach 0.96–1.00, while PCA and k k -means stay
at 0.12–0.36. Retrained DAS lies at a median of 1.9–3.7 times vanilla per size, above every other method on all 19
tasks at each of the five sizes. The order of the positions thus explains the lower published scores of the difference of
means and the probes on these tasks, but on most of them not those of PCA and k k -means.

blocks.en:
The re-run of Section 7.3 covers seven models, each with three initialisations ( Table 10 ). Three
details of the code of Tigges et al. (2024) matter for what the published number measures. First,
the authors’ results script builds Table 1a from the all-position column, taking the maximum over layers. Their text
describes the adjective and verb positions, so only the script shows that the published number comes from a complete cut.
Second, the best-epoch reload restores the saved state dictionaries of the rotation module, which alias its live weights, so
it returns the last epoch. At the selected layer, the directions under the two rules have cosine 0.997 or more and
values within 0.9 points. At other layers, the values differ by up to 20 points. Third, the code
trains the direction by patching it at the adjective alone, a partial cut, so its objective never acts on the complete cut
that the published number reads. We copy the behaviour
of the code, including the orthogonal parametrisation of the rotation, gradient clipping and the seed. Because the table
keeps the best of the layers, the interval at the selected layer accounts for that choice. It is a max-type studentised band,
simultaneous over the layers, on blocks of two neighbouring prompts (11–14 blocks per model). Each bound is at 2.5%,
as for every interval in this paper. Under that band, our run at Pythia-1.4b is consistent with the published value. The band
does not lie above 100% in any model, for any initialisation. The conservative Bonferroni interval does not lie above 100%
in any model either ( Table 10 ). The direction of Pythia-410m has the highest value, 198.8%, with a band
from 91.9 to 271.0%. This result depends on the small-sample correction, which widens both the band and the
Bonferroni interval when there are so few blocks. With u u the number of blocks, the band multiplies the standard
deviation of the resampling by u / ( u − 1 ) \sqrt{u/(u-1)} and its critical value by t 0.975 , u − 1 / z 0.975 t_{0.975,\,u-1}/z_{0.975} . The Bonferroni interval
uses the same scaled standard deviation with Student’s t t on u − 1 u-1 degrees of freedom. Without the correction, the band runs
from 104.8 to 262.3%, above 100% for every initialisation, and the Bonferroni interval lies above
100% too. The band of every other model gives the same result without the correction. The directions from the
three initialisations lie within half a point of each other (198.5 to 199.0%), so the two that we had not
seen when we chose the band cannot test that choice.

blocks.en:
This appendix describes the library of Section 8 in full. Besides the quantities of the three steps of that
section, the library computes those of the theory on the given pairs. For the range of Theorem 5 at a cell or at the readout, it reports the trace, λ 1 \lambda_{1} (with
its interval at the readout), λ D \lambda_{D} and the position of a given direction in the range. The upper end λ 1 \lambda_{1} , the
predicted maximum, is computed before any training and bounds the effect that a rank-one direction can reach to first order.
Inside the network, training exceeds it at some cells ( Section 6.1 ). The value that Proposition 8 computes from a single
angle predicts λ 1 \lambda_{1} on a two-label set, and the trace test of Proposition 10 checks the first-order approximation on
a mirrored set. The library also checks Proposition 3 on the given model. It works on Hugging Face models with the GPT-2, GPT-NeoX (Pythia), Llama, Qwen2 and Gemma-2 architectures (SmolLM2 uses the Llama architecture), loaded with eager
attention. It takes pairs in CausalGym’s format, that
is, a base and a source split into regions, with two single-token labels. It follows the conventions of the paper. Layers and
cells are as in Section 4.2 , the best context is chosen on the training pairs or on the given pairs, effects are in
units of the mean T T , and intervals resample a pair with its mirror 2000 times. The patches need only forward passes. The
range and the angle need one gradient per pair, at the midpoint between the base and source states, and the trace test
needs a second gradient, at the base point. The calls of the library are documented with the code ( Section B.5 ).

blocks.en:
On tiny random models of each family, the test of the library checks three statements exactly. Patching every position of a
layer gives T T , a patch along a pair’s own difference equals whole-state patching, and Theorem 5 (iv) holds for one
pair. On GPT-2, from our pairs and saved directions, the library reproduces the values of our measurement. At the readout of
29 CausalGym tasks, T T and the exact effect of every saved direction on each test pair (104,400 values) agree
within 2.3 × 10 − 4 2.3\times 10^{-4} log odds, and λ 1 \lambda_{1} and the trace agree within 5.5 × 10 − 6 5.5\times 10^{-6} . On the 26 two-label tasks, the
cosine of the angle and the shared fraction of the readout gradients ( Section C.2 ) agree within 1.8 × 10 − 7 1.8\times 10^{-7} . Inside
the network, we compare at the 114 live cells ( Section 6.1 ) below the readout in
three maps. At every cell, the context that the library chooses for G ∗ G^{*} on the training pairs is the same as ours.
The values of G G , of G ∗ G^{*} (in that context and in the context chosen on the test pairs) and of five saved directions, each
measured with attention free and with attention frozen, agree per test pair within 3.3 × 10 − 4 3.3\times 10^{-4} log odds. The value of w ⊤ ​ Δ w^{\top}\Delta agrees per pair within 7.8 × 10 − 4 7.8\times 10^{-4} , and λ 1 \lambda_{1} agrees within 6.6 × 10 − 5 6.6\times 10^{-5} . The library recomputes the
whole-state patches at every cell and the base run with every patch, whereas the scripts behind our maps share these passes.

Consider one cell of a template with R R regions besides the start-of-text region, which is neither mapped
nor used as a context. At this cell, Algorithm 1 runs at most five forward passes with a patch per test pair. Three of
them are for G ∗ G^{*} (the cell alone, and its context alone and together with the cell), one is along the direction, and one is
along the direction with attention frozen. The 2 ​ R − 1 2R-1 patches that choose the context of G ∗ G^{*} (the cell alone, each other
region alone, and each other region together with the cell) run on each training pair. The total effect T T and the base run
take forward passes without a patch, which every cell shares. Over a map, the patches of single regions and of pairs of
regions are shared by every
cell of their layer. This amounts to R ⁡ ( R + 1 ) / 2 R(R+1)/2 whole-state patches per layer and training pair, at most as many on the test
pairs, and 2 ​ R 2R patches along directions per layer and test pair. No gradient is computed, and the direction may come from
any method.
